lessons.briefing: Healthy soil is the foundation of food security. Before a farmer adds any amendment or plants any crop, they must understand what their soil actually is: its texture class, its structure, its organic matter content, and its pH. These four parameters determine water-holding capacity, nutrient availability, and biological activity — the three pillars of soil fertility. All four can be assessed accurately with no laboratory equipment.
lessons.contentMd:
## Soil Mineral Fractions

Mineral soil consists of three particle size classes:

| Fraction | Particle diameter | Properties |
|---|---|---|
| Sand | 0.05 – 2.0 mm | Large pores; drains fast; low CEC; poor water retention |
| Silt | 0.002 – 0.05 mm | Medium pores; moderate drainage; moderate CEC |
| Clay | < 0.002 mm | Tiny pores; drains slowly; high CEC; sticky when wet; cracks when dry |

**Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)**: clay particles carry negative charges that
hold positively charged nutrient cations (K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, NH4+). Higher clay
and organic matter = higher CEC = higher fertility potential.

## USDA Soil Texture Triangle

Twelve texture classes are defined by sand/silt/clay percentages. The three
most important for East African smallholders:

| Texture class | Approx. composition | Farming implication |
|---|---|---|
| Sandy loam | 60% sand, 25% silt, 15% clay | Good drainage; needs frequent irrigation and organic matter |
| Clay loam | 30% sand, 35% silt, 35% clay | Good fertility; may compact; add organic matter for structure |
| Loam | 40% sand, 40% silt, 20% clay | Ideal — balanced drainage, aeration, and fertility |

## Field Ribbon Test (No Equipment)

1. Take a golf-ball-sized soil sample; moisten to consistency of putty
2. Squeeze soil between thumb and forefinger, pushing forward
3. Measure the ribbon length before it breaks:
   - **< 2.5 cm**: Sandy loam or loamy sand — low clay
   - **2.5 – 5.0 cm**: Loam or clay loam — moderate clay
   - **> 5.0 cm**: Clay or silty clay — high clay content
4. Feel the ribbon: gritty = sand dominant; smooth/silky = silt; sticky/plastic = clay

## Jar Sedimentation Test (24-hour)

1. Fill a clear 1-litre jar one-third full with soil
2. Add water to near-full; add 1 teaspoon of salt (flocculates clay)
3. Shake vigorously for 2 minutes; stand undisturbed
4. Measure layer thicknesses after sedimentation:
   - **2 minutes**: sand settles first (bottom layer)
   - **1-2 hours**: silt settles (middle layer)
   - **24 hours**: clay settles (top mineral layer)
   - Organic matter floats
5. Calculate percentages: each layer thickness / total mineral thickness x 100

## Soil Structure

| Structure type | Appearance | Fertility implication |
|---|---|---|
| Granular | Round aggregates, crumbly | Excellent — good pore space, drainage, and root penetration |
| Blocky (angular) | Angular blocks with flat faces | Moderate — common in clay soils; can be improved with organic matter |
| Platy | Flat horizontal layers | Poor — restricts drainage and root growth; often indicates compaction |
| Massive | No visible structure, hard clod | Very poor — compacted or degraded; needs deep tillage and organic matter |

Target structure for crop production: **granular**, at least 20 cm deep.

## Soil Organic Matter (SOM) and Its Role

SOM typically represents 1-5% of soil mass but drives:
- CEC: 1% SOM adds approximately 2-4 cmol/kg CEC (equivalent to high-clay soil)
- Water retention: 1% SOM increase retains approximately 20 L extra water per m2 per 30 cm depth
- Biological activity: carbon source for soil microbes that cycle nutrients

**Visual SOM indicator**: dark brown/black colour in topsoil = high SOM.
Light tan or grey = low SOM. Kenyan smallholder soils typically have < 1% SOM
due to burning, tillage, and residue removal — rebuilding is the central task.

## Soil pH and Nutrient Availability

pH scale runs 0 (acid) to 14 (alkaline); optimal crop range is 6.0-7.0.

| pH range | Nutrient availability | Common in East Africa |
|---|---|---|
| < 5.5 (strongly acid) | Al3+ and Mn2+ toxic; P locked; Mo deficient | Highland tea zones, old volcanic soils |
| 5.5 – 6.5 (slightly acid) | Most nutrients available; ideal for maize | Western Kenya, some Rift Valley |
| 6.5 – 7.5 (neutral) | Optimal availability for all major nutrients | Best farmland; aim for this range |
| > 7.5 (alkaline) | Fe, Mn, B, Zn locked; P precipitates | Semi-arid areas with calcareous soils |

## Field pH Testing

1. Take 1 tablespoon of fresh soil into a white dish
2. Add a few drops of distilled or rain water (not tap water — often pH 7.5+)
3. Dip pH indicator strip into the muddy water for 5 seconds
4. Compare colour against reference chart — read to nearest 0.5 pH unit
5. Repeat with 3 samples across the field; average the readings

## Liming for Acid Soils

Agricultural lime (calcium carbonate, CaCO3) raises soil pH:

| Current pH | Target pH 6.5 | Lime rate (tonnes/ha) for clay loam |
|---|---|---|
| 4.5 | 6.5 | 4-6 t/ha |
| 5.0 | 6.5 | 2-4 t/ha |
| 5.5 | 6.5 | 1-2 t/ha |

Incorporate lime 3-6 months before planting; takes one season to fully react.
Dolomitic lime (CaCO3 + MgCO3) also supplies magnesium — preferred where
magnesium deficiency is common (light green youngest leaves = Mg deficiency).

## Soil Colour and Munsell Chart

Colour tells the story of soil chemistry:
- **Dark brown/black**: high organic matter
- **Red/orange**: well-oxidised iron (good drainage, often acidic)
- **Yellow**: hydrated iron oxides (imperfect drainage)
- **Grey/blue-green mottles**: waterlogged, reducing conditions (poor drainage)
- **White patches**: calcium carbonate accumulation (alkaline)

exercises.explanation:
A ribbon > 5 cm indicates high clay content. Sticky feel confirms clay dominance. Clay soils have high CEC (fertility) but compact easily, drain slowly, and crack when dry. Organic matter additions improve structure and drainage.

Why the other options are wrong: Sandy soils produce ribbons < 2.5 cm and feel gritty. A 6 cm sticky ribbon indicates clay, not sand. Loam ribbons are 2.5-5.0 cm and feel neither particularly gritty nor particularly sticky. 6 cm places this firmly in the clay range. Silt feels silky and smooth, not sticky. A 6 cm ribbon that is sticky indicates clay dominance, not silt.

options.text: Sandy loam — poor water retention; needs frequent irrigation
Loam — ideal balanced soil requiring no amendment
Clay or clay loam — good fertility but prone to compaction and waterlogging; add organic matter to improve structure
Silt loam — silky feel indicates high silt with no drainage concerns

exercises.prompt: A farmer squeezes moistened soil and produces a ribbon of 6 cm before it breaks. The ribbon feels sticky and slightly gritty. What texture class is most likely, and what is the primary farming challenge?

exercises.explanation: Settling time reflects particle size and density: sand (largest) settles fastest, clay (smallest) slowest. pH 6.0-7.0 is optimal because most macro and micronutrients are simultaneously available in this range; outside it, either aluminium toxicity (< 5.5) or iron/zinc lockout (> 7.5) reduces yields.
exercises.prompt: In the 24-hour jar sedimentation test, sand settles within ___ minutes, silt within ___ hours, and clay within ___ hours. The optimal soil pH range for most food crops is ___ to ___.

exercises.explanation: Granular structure is the goal of all soil management. Platy structure is often caused by livestock trampling, heavy machinery, or tillage when soil is too wet. Massive structure indicates severe compaction or destruction of all aggregates.

right.text: Excellent — crumbly aggregates with good pore space for roots and drainage
Poor — horizontal layers restrict drainage and root penetration
Very poor — compacted with no visible structure; needs deep tillage
Moderate — common in clay; improves with organic matter additions

exercises.prompt: Match each soil structure type to its fertility implication.

exercises.explanation:
pH 5.2 is in the 5.0-5.5 range. For clay loam, the Kenya MOH/KALRO guidance recommends 2-4 t/ha CaCO3 to raise to 6.5. Incorporation 3-6 months ahead allows full chemical reaction with the soil before crop establishment.

Why the other options are wrong: Maize optimal pH is 6.0-6.8. Below 5.5, aluminium toxicity reduces root development and phosphorus availability. Sulfur would worsen the problem. pH 5.2 is strongly acid. Aluminium (Al3+) becomes toxic below 5.5, and phosphorus is locked by aluminium ions, significantly reducing maize yields. The correct rate for pH 5.0-5.5 is 2-4 t/ha, not 6-8 t/ha. Over-liming can raise pH above 7.5 causing micronutrient deficiencies. Also, lime must be incorporated 3-6 months before planting to react fully.

options.text: Apply sulfur to lower the pH further — maize prefers acid soils
No action needed — pH 5.2 is adequate for all crops
Apply 2-4 t/ha of agricultural lime, incorporate 3-6 months before planting — this raises pH from 5.0 toward the optimal 6.5
Apply 6-8 t/ha lime immediately before planting for fastest response

exercises.prompt: A field pH test returns 5.2 on clay loam soil destined for maize. What action and approximate lime rate are appropriate?

exercises.explanation: SOM's water retention: 1% SOM holds 20 L/m2/30cm — equivalent to 2 mm of additional rain stored in the root zone. This can extend the effective growing season by days to weeks during dry spells. Kenyan smallholder soils often measure 0.5-0.8% SOM due to residue burning and continuous tillage — rebuilding to 2-3% is achievable with compost additions over 3-5 seasons.
exercises.prompt: Each 1% increase in soil organic matter retains approximately ___ litres of additional water per square metre per 30 cm depth. A typical Kenyan smallholder soil depleted by burning and tillage has SOM below ___%.

lessons.outline: Soil mineral fractions (sand, silt, clay) and texture triangle; field ribbon test and jar sedimentation test; soil structure types (granular, blocky, platy, massive) and their fertility implications; soil organic matter (SOM) and its role in CEC and water retention; pH scale and nutrient availability window; field pH testing with indicator strips; liming (CaCO3) and acidification correction; soil colour and Munsell chart interpretation.
lessons.title: Soil Science — Texture, Structure, pH & Field Testing

lessons.briefing: Compost is the single most powerful and cheapest soil amendment available to African smallholders. A well-managed 1 m3 compost pile converts crop residues, kitchen waste, and animal manure into finished compost in 6-8 weeks — providing organic matter, balanced nutrients, and billions of beneficial microorganisms per gram. This lesson covers the four parameters that control composting speed, the full construction sequence, and three alternative systems for water-scarce or space-limited situations.
lessons.contentMd:
## The Four Composting Parameters

Thermophilic composting reaches 55-70°C when four parameters are in balance:

| Parameter | Optimal range | How to fix if wrong |
|---|---|---|
| C:N ratio | 25:1 to 30:1 | Too high (dry/woody): add green material or manure; Too low (slimy): add straw or dry grass |
| Moisture | 50-60% ("wrung sponge" test) | Too dry: sprinkle water; Too wet: add dry carbon material and turn |
| Aeration | Pile must breathe | Turn pile every 3-5 days; use aeration pipes if large pile |
| Particle size | 2-5 cm (chopped) | Large pieces: chop with panga or machete before adding |

**Wrung sponge test**: grab a handful of compost material and squeeze firmly.
If water drips freely — too wet. If no moisture felt in palm — too dry.
If just a few drops express — correct moisture.

## Common C:N Ratios

| Material | C:N ratio | Category |
|---|---|---|
| Fresh grass clippings | 15:1 | Green (N-rich) |
| Vegetable kitchen scraps | 15:1 | Green |
| Cattle manure | 20:1 | Green/balanced |
| Coffee grounds | 20:1 | Green |
| Straw/dry grass | 80:1 | Brown (C-rich) |
| Dry leaves | 60:1 | Brown |
| Sawdust | 400:1 | Brown |
| Newspaper | 170:1 | Brown |

Rule of thumb: **3 parts brown to 1 part green by volume** achieves
approximately 25-30:1 C:N for most mixed farm waste.

## Compost Pile Construction (Berkeley 18-Day Method)

1. Choose a shaded site; lay 10 cm of coarse woody material as base (airflow)
2. Layer brown material (20 cm) then green material (10 cm), alternating
3. Moisten each layer as you build — target wrung-sponge moisture throughout
4. Total pile size: minimum 1 m x 1 m x 1 m (critical mass for heat)
5. Maximum size: 2 m wide x 1.5 m high (too big restricts core aeration)
6. Insert a wooden probe at pile centre as thermometer guide
7. Cover with jute sack or grass thatch to retain moisture and heat

### Turning Schedule for Rapid (18-Day) Compost

| Day | Action | Expected temperature |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Build pile | 20-30°C (ambient) |
| 2-3 | No action | Rises to 50-60°C |
| 4 | First turn — move outer edges to centre | 55-65°C |
| 7 | Second turn | 60-70°C peak |
| 10 | Third turn | 55-65°C |
| 13 | Fourth turn | 40-50°C (cooling) |
| 18 | Final assessment | < 35°C = finished |

**Thermophilic kill**: sustained 55°C for 3 days kills E. coli, Salmonella,
most weed seeds, and most plant pathogens. Ascaris eggs require 60°C or
longer exposure (see Day 4, Part 7).

## Finished Compost Quality Indicators

Good finished compost:
- Dark brown/black colour (no recognisable original materials)
- Earthy smell (not ammonia, not putrid)
- Temperature < 35°C even after moistening and covering
- Crumbly texture — no slimy or fibrous zones
- pH 6.5-8.0 (neutral to slightly alkaline)

Typical finished compost nutrient content (per tonne):
- N: 10-15 kg (mostly organic N — slow release)
- P: 4-8 kg
- K: 8-15 kg
- Plus micronutrients and 200-400 billion CFU of beneficial bacteria per gram

Application rate: 5-10 t/ha incorporated before planting, or 2-3 kg
per planting hole.

## Compost Tea

Compost tea extracts soluble nutrients and beneficial microbes for foliar or
soil drench application:

1. Fill a 20 L bucket 20% full with mature compost
2. Fill to top with non-chlorinated water (rainwater or borehole water)
3. Aerate with a fish-tank air pump for 24 hours (aerobic tea — higher
   beneficial microbial counts)
4. Strain through cloth; apply undiluted to soil or dilute 1:5 for foliar spray
5. Apply within 4 hours of finishing — microbes die quickly once aeration stops

## Bokashi Fermentation (Kitchen Waste)

Bokashi uses effective microorganisms (EM) — mainly Lactobacillus, yeasts, and
photosynthetic bacteria — to ferment kitchen waste including meat and dairy
(unlike aerobic compost which cannot accept these):

1. Layer kitchen waste in an airtight bucket with bokashi bran (EM-inoculated wheat bran)
2. Compress each layer firmly to exclude air; seal bucket after each addition
3. After 2 weeks at room temperature: pre-compost is ready (pH 4 — very acidic)
4. Bury pre-compost 20 cm deep in soil; it fully breaks down in 2-4 weeks
5. Do NOT apply directly to plant roots — acid pre-compost burns

## Biochar — Soil Carbon Amendment

Biochar is charcoal made by pyrolysing biomass at 400-700°C with limited oxygen
(not burned to ash). Properties:

- Highly porous: 1 g biochar has up to 200 m2 internal surface area
- Stable carbon: persists in soil 100-1,000 years (sequesters carbon)
- Does NOT itself provide nutrients — must be charged with compost or manure
- Increases CEC by 20-30% in sandy soils
- Increases water retention in sandy soils

**Production**: flame-curtain kiln (TLUD — top-lit updraft); cover fire with
soil as soon as flames change from yellow to blue to quench without burning to ash.

**Application**: charge by soaking in compost tea or mixing with manure for
2 weeks before soil application at 1-5 t/ha.

exercises.explanation:
Ammonia smell indicates excess nitrogen being lost as NH3 gas — classic sign of a C:N ratio below 20:1. Low temperature means decomposition is not generating sufficient heat. Adding brown carbon-rich material (straw, 80:1 C:N) and turning corrects both issues.

Why the other options are wrong: A dry pile would show low temperature and an earthy or dusty smell, not ammonia. Ammonia specifically indicates nitrogen excess from too much green material. Ammonia loss = too much N already. Adding more green material would make the ammonia problem worse, not better. By Day 4-7, a well-managed compost pile should reach 55-70°C. 32°C indicates the pile is not thermophilic — the imbalanced C:N is preventing the microbial bloom needed for heat generation.

options.text: Pile is too dry — add water to reach correct moisture
Pile needs more green material — the C:N is too high
C:N ratio is too low (too much green/N material) — turn pile and add dry straw or dry leaves to raise C:N
Temperature is correct — 32°C is normal for Day 6

exercises.prompt: A compost pile on Day 6 measures only 32°C at the centre and smells of ammonia. What is the most likely cause and the correct fix?

exercises.explanation: Minimum 1 m3 is required to generate and retain sufficient heat for the thermophilic microbial community. Smaller piles lose heat faster than they generate it. The 200-400 billion CFU/g figure explains why compost is a microbial inoculant as much as a nutrient source — reseeding degraded soils with soil life is as important as adding N, P, and K.
exercises.prompt: The minimum pile volume for thermophilic (hot) composting is ___ cubic metre.

exercises.explanation: Each system targets a different situation. Hot composting is the workhorse for bulk farm waste. Bokashi solves the kitchen-waste problem. Compost tea provides a fast-acting liquid amendment between solid compost applications. Biochar is a 100-1000 year carbon investment that changes soil structure.

right.text: Large volumes of farm waste; pathogen kill needed; 18-day turnaround
Kitchen waste including meat and dairy; airtight bucket; no smell
Quick foliar or soil drench; delivers soluble nutrients and microbes
Long-term carbon sequestration and CEC improvement in sandy soils

exercises.prompt: Match each composting system to its best use case.

exercises.explanation:
Fresh biochar is a highly adsorptive carbon sponge. If applied uncharged, it will strip plant-available N, P, and K from the soil solution, causing temporary nutrient deficiency (sometimes called the 'biochar hunger'). Charging fills the pores with nutrients before application.

Why the other options are wrong: Biochar is not toxic to soil microbes. In fact, its porous structure provides ideal habitat for bacteria and fungi after charging. The concern is nutrient adsorption, not toxicity. Biochar pH is typically 7-10 depending on production temperature, but at field application rates (1-5 t/ha) the pH effect on soil is minimal. The buffering concern is not the primary reason for charging. Activated carbon is a different product made at higher temperatures with steam activation. Composting-based charging fills biochar pores with nutrients and microbes — it does not change the physical structure.

options.text: Biochar itself contains no nutrients — its porous structure initially adsorbs existing soil nutrients, temporarily reducing plant-available fertility until charged
Biochar is toxic to soil microbes and must be neutralised with compost
Biochar raises soil pH above 9.0 and must be buffered before application
Charging converts biochar into activated carbon for better filtration

exercises.prompt: Why must biochar be charged with compost or manure before soil application?

exercises.explanation: Compost tea microbes die within 4 hours once the aerator is removed — the high microbial count is only maintained while oxygen is supplied. Bokashi pH of 4 is highly acidic — direct root contact would burn. Burying 20 cm deep protects roots while the acid pre-compost is rapidly neutralised and broken down by soil microbes over 2-4 weeks.
exercises.prompt: Compost tea should be applied within ___ hours of finishing aeration. Bokashi pre-compost has a pH of approximately ___ and must be buried at least ___ cm deep to avoid burning plant roots.

lessons.outline: The four composting control parameters (C:N ratio, moisture, aeration, particle size); hot aerobic composting — pile construction and turning schedule; temperature monitoring and thermophilic pathogen kill; finished compost quality indicators; compost tea production and application; bokashi fermentation for kitchen waste; vermicompost integration; biochar — production and soil amendment properties; liquid manure (slurry) from cattle dung.
lessons.title: Composting & Organic Soil Amendments

lessons.briefing: In semi-arid Kenya, where rainfall is bimodal, erratic, and declining, the difference between food security and food crisis is often 50 mm of rain that runs off bare, compacted soil rather than soaking in. Water-wise farming techniques — zai pits, half-moon catchments, contour swales, and low-cost drip irrigation — capture, store, and deliver every raindrop to the root zone of the crop, multiplying the effective rainfall by 2-4 times.
lessons.contentMd:
## Rainfall and Runoff

Kenya's semi-arid areas receive 400-700 mm of annual rainfall, yet crop yields
are often equivalent to what 150-200 mm of effective rainfall would support.
The gap is lost water: runoff, evaporation, and deep drainage below the root zone.

| Loss pathway | Typical % of rainfall lost | Intervention |
|---|---|---|
| Runoff (bare soil) | 30-60% | Zai pits, swales, tied ridges |
| Evaporation (bare soil surface) | 20-40% | Mulching, minimum tillage |
| Deep drainage (sandy soils) | 5-20% | Biochar, organic matter |
| Crop transpiration (desired) | 20-40% | — |

**Infiltration rate** of compacted crusted soil: 2-5 mm/hour.
Healthy soil with good structure: 20-50 mm/hour. During a 30-minute storm
delivering 20 mm of rain, compacted soil absorbs only 1-2.5 mm — the rest
runs off carrying topsoil.

## Zai Pits

Originally from Burkina Faso (Yacouba Sawadogo), adapted across the Sahel.
Zai pits are hand-dug micro-catchments that concentrate water and organic
matter at the seed point.

### Design Specifications

- **Pit dimensions**: 30 cm wide x 30 cm long x 15 cm deep
- **Spacing**: 0.9 m between pits in rows; 0.9 m between rows (1 pit per 0.81 m2)
- **Density**: approximately 12,300 pits per hectare
- **Soil placement**: excavated soil forms a downslope crescent bund (catches runoff)
- **Organic fill**: add 1-2 handfuls of compost or manure per pit before planting
- **Termite attraction**: manure fills attract termites which channel additional water to 40+ cm depth

### Yield Impact

In trials across semi-arid East Africa, zai pits increase sorghum and millet
yields by 40-100% compared to flat planting in the same rainfall conditions.
In severe drought years, crops on zai pits often produce while flat-planted
crops fail entirely.

## Half-Moon Catchments (Demi-Lunes)

Used for trees and large shrubs in drylands:

- Semicircular earth bund, flat side upslope, curved bund downslope
- Diameter: 2-4 m per demi-lune
- Plants at the centre of the flat base
- One demi-lune catches runoff from an upslope area 3-5x its own size

## Contour Swales

A swale is a level trench dug exactly on the contour (zero slope) with the
excavated soil forming a downslope berm:

### A-Frame Level Construction

1. Cut two equal legs (1.5 m each) and one crossbar (1.5 m) into an A-frame
2. Hang a plumb line (stone + string) from the apex
3. Mark where plumb hits crossbar when both legs are on flat ground
4. Walk the A-frame along the slope: the contour is the line where the
   plumb bob rests on the same mark
5. Mark with stakes every 2-3 m; connect stakes with a hoe trench

### Swale Specifications

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Trench depth | 30-50 cm |
| Trench width | 50-100 cm |
| Berm height | 30-40 cm above downslope ground |
| Spacing between swales | 3-10 m vertically (depends on slope steepness) |
| Overflow spillway | Always include — 20 cm lower section to prevent berm breach |

Swales capture runoff, allow it to infiltrate slowly, and recharge
groundwater. Trees planted on the berm access this stored moisture
during dry spells.

## Low-Cost Drip Irrigation

### Jerrycan Gravity Drip (Household Scale)

- 20 L jerrycan elevated 1 m above ground on a stand
- 0.5 mm holes (use hot nail or drill bit) in a 15 mm PE pipe connected at bottom
- One jerrycan irrigates approximately 25 plants at 0.5 L each per filling
- Flow rate: 0.5 mm holes deliver approximately 30 mL/hour at 1 m head
- Irrigation interval: every 2-3 days for most crops in warm lowlands

### Bucket Drip Kit (0.1-0.4 ha scale)

Commercial bucket drip kits (KickStart, IDE) use:
- 20 L elevated bucket or small tank (200-1,000 L)
- Mainline PE pipe (16 mm) with lateral lines (12 mm) every 60 cm
- Button emitters or punch-hole emitters at 30-60 cm spacing
- Pressure filter on inlet to prevent clogging
- Cost: approximately KES 3,000-12,000 for a 0.1-0.2 ha kit

Water savings versus flood irrigation: 30-50% less water for same yield.

## Mulching

Mulch reduces surface evaporation, moderates soil temperature, suppresses
weeds, and slowly adds organic matter as it decomposes.

| Mulch type | Depth | Evaporation reduction |
|---|---|---|
| Dry grass/straw | 5-10 cm | 50-70% |
| Crop residues | 5-8 cm | 40-60% |
| Wood chips | 8-12 cm | 60-75% |
| Living mulch (creeping legume) | Ground cover | 40-60% + nitrogen fixation |

Apply mulch leaving a 5 cm gap around stem base to prevent rot and rodent shelter.

## Tied Ridges

Ridges formed between crop rows are tied at 2-5 m intervals with small earth
dams (ties), converting furrows into a series of small water storage basins:

- Each basin captures 2-5 L of runoff before overflowing to the next
- Labour: approximately 3 person-days per hectare to tie ridges
- Yield improvement in semi-arid areas: 30-60% over open ridges

exercises.explanation:
If the storm delivers 30 mm in 30 min = 60 mm/hour rain rate. Infiltration is only 3 mm/hour. In 30 min, 1.5 mm infiltrates while 28.5 mm runs off = 95% loss. This is why crusted, bare soil is catastrophic in semi-arid areas — virtually all rain is lost.

Why the other options are wrong: 50% absorption assumes around 30 mm/hour infiltration rate. Compacted crusted soil only achieves 2-5 mm/hour. At 3 mm/hour in a 30-minute storm, only ~5% infiltrates. Semi-arid rainfall is often intense and convective. High-intensity short-duration storms are the norm, and they overwhelm the infiltration capacity of bare compacted soils, producing flash runoff. Evaporation occurs over hours to days, not during the storm itself. During the storm, the primary loss mechanism is runoff. 30% runoff would require an infiltration rate of ~42 mm/hour — not possible on compacted crust.

options.text: Approximately 50% runs off — most soils absorb at least half of incoming rain
No runoff occurs — rain in semi-arid areas is always light and absorbed fully
About 30% runs off — the remainder is lost to evaporation
The storm delivers 30 mm in roughly 30 minutes; at 3 mm/hour absorption rate only about 1.5 mm infiltrates — approximately 95% runs off

exercises.prompt: A farmer has a 0.25 ha plot on a 5% slope in a semi-arid area receiving 500 mm of annual rain. During a 30 mm rainstorm, the compacted crusted soil absorbs only 3 mm/hour. Approximately what percentage of this storm's rain is lost to runoff?

exercises.explanation: 30x30x15 cm pits at 0.9 m x 0.9 m spacing gives 1/0.81 = 1.235 pits per m2, so 12,350 pits per hectare (commonly rounded to 12,300). Each pit receives a handful of manure before planting, creating a microhabitat of concentrated fertility and water at every seed point.
exercises.prompt: Standard zai pits are ___ cm wide x ___ cm long x ___ cm deep, spaced ___ m apart in all directions. At this spacing there are approximately ___ pits per hectare.

exercises.explanation: These techniques act at different scales: zai pits at the individual plant, tied ridges at the row, swales at the field/catchment. They can be combined — swales intercept hillslope runoff that is then distributed to zai-pit fields below.

right.text: Concentrate runoff and organic matter at individual plant points on degraded crusted soil
Intercept hillslope runoff along the contour and allow slow infiltration to recharge groundwater
Convert inter-row furrows into a series of small water-retention basins between tie dams
Reduce surface evaporation by 50-75% while adding organic matter as it decomposes

exercises.prompt: Match each water-wise technique to its primary mechanism of action.

exercises.explanation:
30 mL/hour x 6 hours = 180 mL. A fruiting tomato needs 1,000-2,000 mL/day. Multiple emitters per plant or longer run time is needed. Jerrycan drip is best for seedlings or drought-stressed crops receiving supplemental irrigation, not sole-source irrigation for heavy feeders.

Why the other options are wrong: 180 mL is far below the 1,000-2,000 mL/day mature tomatoes require. Jerrycan drip provides supplemental irrigation — it must be paired with rain-fed or higher-volume supply for fruiting crops. Volume delivered = flow rate x time. 30 mL/hour x 6 hours = 180 mL. The accumulative volume over time is what reaches the plant. 180 mL = 0.18 L, not 1.8 L. 1.8 L would require 300 mL/hour flow rate, which is much larger than a 0.5 mm hole at 1 m head delivers.

options.text: 180 mL per emitter per 6-hour session — mature tomatoes need 1-2 L/day so 2-3 sessions per day or longer run time is needed
180 mL — this fully meets mature tomato water needs
30 mL — the system only delivers at the flow rate, not accumulative
1.8 L — units must be converted from mL to L

exercises.prompt: A household sets up a jerrycan gravity drip system with 0.5 mm holes in the lateral pipe, elevated 1 m. Each hole delivers approximately 30 mL/hour. If the system runs for 6 hours, how much water does one emitter deliver, and is this sufficient for a mature tomato plant?

exercises.explanation: A contour is a line of equal elevation — water placed on a true contour swale spreads evenly left and right with no tendency to flow. An overflow spillway 20 cm lower than the berm crest ensures that when the swale fills in a major storm, water exits in a controlled location rather than overtopping and eroding the berm catastrophically.
exercises.prompt: The A-frame level is used to mark the ___ (gradient = zero) line on a hillslope for swale construction. A swale berm must always include an ___ spillway section ___ cm lower than the main berm to prevent catastrophic failure during heavy rain.

lessons.briefing: Agroforestry — integrating trees with crops and livestock — is the most documented path to long-term soil fertility restoration in East Africa. Nitrogen-fixing trees deliver 50-200 kg of biologically fixed nitrogen per hectare per year through their root nodules, replacing expensive synthetic fertiliser. Properly designed agroforestry systems also provide fuelwood, fodder, shade, windbreaks, and improved water infiltration — all from trees already growing on the farm.
lessons.contentMd:
## Biological Nitrogen Fixation

Nitrogen fixation is the conversion of atmospheric N2 (78% of air) into
plant-available ammonium (NH4+) by the nitrogenase enzyme in Rhizobium bacteria
living symbiotically in root nodules of leguminous plants.

**The process:**
1. Legume root exudates attract compatible Rhizobium from soil
2. Bacteria infect root hair and form a nodule (2-10 mm diameter pink/red inside)
3. Inside the nodule: N2 + 8H+ + 8e- + 16 ATP → 2 NH3 + H2 + 16 ADP
4. Ammonia converted to ammonium (NH4+), absorbed by plant
5. When roots decompose, fixed N enters the soil

**Pink/red nodule interior = active fixation** (contains leghaemoglobin).
White or brown inside = inactive or dead nodule (poor soil, wrong Rhizobium strain).

Annual N fixation rates by species in East Africa:

| Species | N fixed (kg/ha/year) |
|---|---|
| Leucaena leucocephala | 100-500 kg/ha |
| Calliandra calothyrsus | 50-150 kg/ha |
| Gliricidia sepium | 80-200 kg/ha |
| Sesbania sesban (short-cycle) | 40-200 kg/ha |
| Tithonia diversifolia (shrub) | 20-100 kg/ha |
| Climbing beans (crop) | 50-150 kg/ha |

## Key N-Fixing Species for East Africa

### Calliandra calothyrsus (Red Calliandra)
- Multi-purpose: fodder (35% crude protein), fuelwood, erosion control
- Tolerates: acid soils (pH 4.5-7.0), waterlogged soils, altitudes to 2,400 m
- Management: coppice to 0.5 m every 2-3 months for fodder production
- Green leaf application: 2-4 t/ha fresh biomass adds 40-80 kg N/ha

### Leucaena leucocephala (White Leadtree)
- Highest N fixation rate (100-500 kg N/ha/year)
- Fast-growing: 3-5 m in first year; coppices vigorously
- Limitations: intolerant of acid soils (pH < 5.5); mimosine in leaves
  toxic to non-ruminants and ruminants without adapted gut bacteria
- Best for: alley cropping in medium-altitude neutral-pH areas

### Tithonia diversifolia (Mexican Sunflower)
- Shrubby perennial, not a legume — fixes N via mycorrhizal partnerships
- Very high biomass N content: 3.5-4.5% N in leaves (similar to synthetic urea)
- Grow on field edges; cut and carry as green manure
- Application: 2-5 t/ha fresh biomass incorporated before planting adds
  70-200 kg N equivalent per hectare

### Sesbania sesban (Improved Fallow)
- Short-cycle tree (1-2 year fallow): plant after harvest, cut before next season
- Produces 40-200 kg N/ha in one fallow season
- Trials in western Kenya: following 2-year Sesbania fallow, maize yields
  4-6 t/ha without fertiliser vs 0.5-1.5 t/ha in unfallowed control plots

## Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR)

FMNR is the deliberate protection and management of naturally regenerating
trees and shrubs on farmland by pruning suckers to a single strong stem:

1. Select strongest sucker from stumps already present in the field
2. Remove competing shoots; protect from grazing for first year
3. Prune lower branches at 1.5-2.0 m height once established
4. Trees provide shade, N, roots to fight erosion, and fuelwood from prunings

FMNR cost: near zero (trees already exist). Impact: demonstrated to restore
5 million ha of degraded Sahel farmland with 500,000 farm families.

## Alley Cropping Design

In alley cropping, rows of N-fixing trees are planted at regular intervals
with food crops grown between them:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Tree row spacing | 4-8 m apart (wider spacing = less shading of crops) |
| Tree spacing within row | 0.25-0.5 m (dense hedge) |
| Pollarding height | 0.5-1.0 m above ground when cutting |
| Cutting frequency | At planting + 6-8 weeks later (when maize is knee-high) |
| Biomass placement | Lay prunings on soil surface as mulch; or incorporate |

The tree biomass from 4-8 m alleys in a 1 ha field provides approximately
60-180 kg N equivalent per hectare per year if harvested and incorporated.

## Legume Intercropping

Short-cycle annual legumes grown with staple cereals provide dual benefits:
nitrogen fixation during the season + grain protein harvest.

| Cereal | Intercrop legume | Arrangement |
|---|---|---|
| Maize | Climbing bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) | Bean planted 2 weeks after maize, uses maize stalk as support |
| Sorghum | Cowpea (Vigna unguiculata) | Sow cowpea in alternate rows; cowpea tolerates drought |
| Millet | Groundnut (Arachis hypogaea) | Groundnut fixes 50-150 kg N/ha; also enriches diet |
| Maize | Desmodium (Silverleaf) | Push-pull system — Desmodium repels striga and stem borers |

**Push-Pull System** (ICIPE, Kenya): Desmodium intercrop repels stem borers
(push); Napier grass planted around field perimeter attracts stem borers away
from maize (pull). Also suppresses Striga weed through allelopathy.
Yield improvements: 2-3x in heavily infested fields.

exercises.explanation:
Active nodules contain leghaemoglobin which gives a pink/red colour. White or grey interior indicates the Rhizobium are absent, dead, or inactive. Causes include: wrong Rhizobium strain, soil pH < 5.5 (kills Rhizobium), waterlogging, or high soil nitrogen (N inhibits fixation when fertiliser N is abundant).

Why the other options are wrong: This is incorrect. Pink/red colour from leghaemoglobin is the indicator of active fixation. White or grey indicates inactive nodules. Active nodules are pink/red from early establishment. White nodules in mature trees indicate a problem, not a developmental stage. Size does not predict activity. Colour is the key indicator: pink/red = active, white/grey = inactive, regardless of size.

options.text: White nodules indicate maximum nitrogen fixation — the colour shows pure NH3 production
White nodules are normal in young trees — they turn pink after 6 months
Only nodule size matters — small white nodules will fix more N than large pink ones
White/grey nodules are inactive — no nitrogen fixation occurring; check soil pH (Leucaena requires pH > 5.5), consider Rhizobium inoculant on seeds of replacement plants

exercises.prompt: A farmer cuts open a root nodule from a Leucaena tree and finds the interior is white/grey in colour. What does this indicate and what action should be taken?

exercises.explanation: At 4% N (midpoint) in fresh biomass (approximately 25% DM): 3 t/ha fresh x 0.25 DM fraction = 0.75 t/ha dry matter. 0.75 t DM x 40 kg N/t DM (at 4% N) = 30 kg N — but fresh weight at 3.5-4.5% N on fresh weight basis: 3,000 kg x 0.04 = 120 kg N. Range 3.5-4.5% gives 105-135 kg N equivalent per ha. A powerful free fertiliser from a plant that grows on degraded land margins.
exercises.prompt: Tithonia diversifolia leaves contain ___ to ___% nitrogen by dry weight, similar to synthetic urea. Applying 3 t/ha of fresh Tithonia biomass provides approximately ___ kg of nitrogen equivalent per hectare.

exercises.explanation: Matching species to site and farming system is critical. Leucaena fails on acid soils (pH < 5.5) where Calliandra thrives. Sesbania is for the farmer who can afford one fallow season. Desmodium is for maize-belt farmers with stem borer and Striga pressure.

right.text: Highest N fixation rate (100-500 kg/ha/year) for alley cropping on neutral soils
Tolerates acid soils and waterlogging; 35% crude protein fodder for dairy cattle
Short 1-2 year improved fallow that delivers 40-200 kg N before next maize crop
Push-pull intercrop — repels stem borers and suppresses Striga weed

exercises.prompt: Match each agroforestry species to its primary advantage in East Africa.

exercises.explanation:
Desmodium (silverleaf) releases isothiocyanates that push stem borer moths away from the maize stand. Napier grass at borders produces a sticky exudate that traps stem borer larvae after hatching, acting as a dead-end trap crop. This also suppresses Striga through allelopathic root exudates.

Why the other options are wrong: Desmodium does not directly kill insects — it repels them through volatile chemicals. Napier grass does not form a physical barrier; it attracts and traps larvae biochemically. Desmodium does fix some nitrogen as a legume, but the primary purpose of this system is pest and Striga management. Napier grass is a C4 grass and does not fix nitrogen. The mechanism is chemical, not physical shading. The parasitic wasp habitat aspect has some truth but is not the primary mechanism. The core is push (volatile repellent) and pull (attractive trap crop).

options.text: Desmodium kills stem borers with natural insecticide; Napier grass blocks physical entry into the field
Both Desmodium and Napier grass fix nitrogen — the system is primarily for soil fertility
Desmodium releases volatile compounds that repel stem borers away from maize (push); Napier grass attracts stem borers to the field border where they lay eggs but larvae survive poorly (pull)
Napier grass shades stem borer pupae preventing emergence; Desmodium provides habitat for parasitic wasps

exercises.prompt: In the push-pull pest management system, what role does Desmodium intercropped with maize play, and what does the Napier grass border do?

exercises.explanation: Alley spacing of 4-8 m allows adequate light to reach inter-row crops while providing significant N-fixing tree biomass. Pollarding at 0.5-1.0 m keeps trees as hedges rather than large shade trees. FMNR's near-zero cost arises because farmers protect and manage stumps already present in their fields — no tree nursery, no planting, no seedling cost.
exercises.prompt: In alley cropping with Leucaena rows spaced ___ to ___ metres apart, trees are pollarded to ___ to ___ metre height. FMNR costs approximately ___ per hectare since it manages trees that are already ___ on the farmland.

lessons.outline: Biological nitrogen fixation mechanism (Rhizobium nodules, nitrogenase enzyme); key N-fixing species for East Africa (Calliandra calothyrsus, Leucaena leucocephala, Tithonia diversifolia, Sesbania sesban, Gliricidia sepium); improved fallow with Sesbania; fertiliser trees as green manure; Farmer Managed Natural Regeneration (FMNR); alley cropping design (tree rows 6m apart, pollarding height 0.5-1.0m); windbreak design; multi-purpose tree selection; legume intercropping.

lessons.briefing: Seed sovereignty — the ability of farmers to save, replant, and exchange their own seed — is the deepest form of food security. Open-pollinated varieties (OPVs) reproduce true to type from saved seed, unlike F1 hybrids which must be purchased every season. This lesson covers the science of seed selection, processing, storage, and variety trials that enable a community to build a locally adapted, high-yielding seed bank without dependency on commercial suppliers.
lessons.contentMd:
## Open-Pollinated Varieties vs F1 Hybrids

| Feature | Open-Pollinated Variety (OPV) | F1 Hybrid |
|---|---|---|
| Genetics | Genetically diverse, stable lines | Crossing two inbred parental lines |
| Seed saving | Yes — offspring same as parent | No — offspring segregate, lose vigour |
| Yield potential | Good (typically 70-85% of hybrid) | High in ideal conditions |
| Stress resilience | Often better (genetic diversity) | Often poorer (narrow gene base) |
| Seed cost | Near zero (farm-saved) | High — purchased every season |
| Local adaptation | Builds over generations of selection | Fixed at breeding station |

**Key principle**: Saving seed from F1 hybrids produces F2 offspring with
80% reduction in favourable trait combinations (heterozygosity lost). Do not
save from hybrids — always save from OPVs.

## Positive Mass Selection

Mass selection is the most practical seed-saving method for smallholders:

1. Walk the field at maturity — before any harvest begins
2. Identify the **top 10-15% of plants** showing:
   - Tall, straight, unblemished stalks
   - Largest cob/pod/head for the variety
   - Early uniform maturity (same date as neighbours)
   - Disease-free leaves — no rust, blight, or viral lesions
   - Root stability — not lodged even in wind or wet
3. Mark selected plants with a strip of cloth tied to stem
4. Harvest marked plants separately, first, before main harvest begins
5. Dry separately, process separately, store in labelled container

Over 3-5 seasons of consistent positive selection, local yields improve
measurably as the seed population adapts to local conditions.

## Isolation Distances for Cross-Pollinating Crops

Cross-pollinating crops require spatial or temporal isolation to maintain
variety purity:

| Crop | Pollination mechanism | Minimum isolation distance |
|---|---|---|
| Maize | Wind-pollinated | 200-500 m from other maize varieties |
| Sorghum | Mainly self; some cross | 100-200 m |
| Brassicas (kale, cabbage) | Insect-pollinated | 500-1,000 m from other Brassica spp. |
| Sunflower | Insect-pollinated | 1,000 m |
| Squash/pumpkin | Insect-pollinated | 500-1,000 m |
| Tomato | Mainly self-pollinated | 5-10 m (sufficient for most purposes) |
| Beans (common) | Self-pollinated | 5-10 m |
| Cowpea | Self-pollinated | 10-20 m |

For communities without large isolation distances, use **time isolation**:
stagger planting by more than the silk-to-pollen synchrony window (10-14 days
for maize) so varieties flower at different times.

## Seed Drying to Safe Moisture Content

Seeds at high moisture content deteriorate rapidly from mould and respiration.

| Crop category | Safe moisture content | Drying method |
|---|---|---|
| Cereals (maize, sorghum, millet) | < 12% | Sun-dry on raised platforms 3-7 days; test with teeth (hard, no dent = ready) |
| Legumes (beans, cowpea, groundnut) | < 8% | Sun-dry until pods rattle; shell and dry shelled seed further 1-2 days |
| Vegetables (tomato, kale, onion) | < 6% | Shade-dry (UV damages small seeds); 7-14 days on cloth |

**Moisture indicator**: place dried seed in an airtight jar for 24 hours.
If condensation appears on inner jar walls — moisture too high. Continue drying.

## Hermetic Storage

Hermetic storage creates an oxygen-depleted, CO2-rich environment that:
- Kills storage insects (weevils, beetles, bruchid beetles on legumes)
- Prevents moisture re-absorption
- Inhibits mould growth

| Storage container | Capacity | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| PICS triple-layer hermetic bag | 100 kg | Standard for cereal; inexpensive |
| Purdue Improved Cowpea Storage (PICS) | 100 kg | Specifically for legumes; bruchid control |
| Metal drum with sealed lid | 50-200 kg | Very durable; paint to reduce heat absorption |
| Glass jar with rubber seal | 0.5-5 kg | Ideal for small vegetable seed lots |

Add **fresh dry wood ash** (1% by weight) to seed before sealing — raises
pH, desiccates microenvironment, repels insects mechanically.

## Germination (Viability) Test

Before planting, always test seed viability:

1. Count out exactly 50 seeds from your saved stock
2. Lay on moist paper towel; fold over; place in a warm location (25-30°C)
3. Keep moist (not waterlogged) for the crop's germination period:
   - Maize: 5-7 days
   - Beans: 5-7 days
   - Tomato: 7-10 days
4. Count germinated seeds (radicle visible, > 5 mm long)
5. Germination rate = germinated / 50 x 100%

**Decision guide:**
- > 85%: Excellent seed — plant at normal seeding rate
- 70-85%: Good seed — increase seeding rate by 15-20%
- 50-70%: Marginal — increase seeding rate by 30-50% and source new seed
- < 50%: Discard — unacceptably low germination; do not plant

## Community Seed Bank Design

A community seed bank collects, stores, and distributes diverse local varieties:

1. **Storage room**: cool, dry, well-ventilated; insulated walls reduce temperature swings
2. **Inventory**: each variety labelled with: name, collector, village, harvest year, germination rate
3. **Withdrawal policy**: members borrow 1 kg, return 2 kg after harvest (grain-for-grain-plus-surplus)
4. **Refresh cycle**: refresh stored seed every 2-3 years with fresh well-dried stock
5. **Diversity targets**: minimum 3 varieties per crop species; prioritise rare local varieties

## Mother-Baby Variety Trial

A structured on-farm trial to compare varieties under farmer conditions:

- **Mother trial**: one farmer manages all varieties under identical management; generates robust comparison data
- **Baby trials**: 20-30 farmers each grow one new variety alongside their local check in split plot
- Data collection: plant height, days to flowering, days to maturity, yield per plot
- Yield calculation: (harvest weight kg) / (plot area m2) x 10,000 = kg/ha

Results are shared at community field day. Farmers themselves vote on preferred
variety based on yield, taste, storability, and market price.

exercises.explanation:
F1 hybrids exploit heterosis from crossing two inbred parental lines. F2 offspring (from saved F1 seed) undergo Mendelian segregation, with 75% of gene pairs becoming homozygous. Favourable dominant-dominant combinations drop from ~100% to ~56% in F2, producing dramatically lower and uneven yields.

Why the other options are wrong: Adaptation through selection takes many generations and requires genetic diversity. F1 hybrids start with limited diversity, and segregation in F2/F3 primarily produces poorly performing homozygous lines, not adapted ones. F1 yield advantage specifically comes from the first-generation heterozygosity. Saving seed destroys this advantage. Commercial seed companies rely on this biological fact to maintain annual seed purchase dependency. All traits that benefit from heterozygosity — including yield, stress tolerance, and disease resistance — decline in F2 generation. It is not selective loss of disease resistance only.

options.text: Yields improve season by season as the plants adapt to local conditions
Yields stay the same — F1 seed and saved seed from F1 perform identically
Only the disease resistance is lost; yield potential is maintained through saving
Yields decline sharply in F2 and F3 generations as heterozygosity is lost — offspring no longer have the favourable gene combinations of the original hybrid cross

exercises.prompt: A farmer saves seed from an F1 hybrid maize variety for three seasons running. What happens to the crop performance, and why?

exercises.explanation: Maize is wind-pollinated over 200-500 m. Below 12% moisture, weevils cannot complete their life cycle and mould is suppressed. Germination: 38/50 x 100 = 76% — falls in the 70-85% marginal-to-good range. Increase seeding rate by 15-20% and plan to source better seed for the next season.
exercises.prompt: Maize seed for saving must be isolated at least ___ metres from other maize varieties to prevent cross-pollination. Safe moisture content for stored maize seed is below ___%. A germination test using 50 seeds returns 38 germinated — the germination rate is ___% and the recommendation is ___.

exercises.explanation: Isolation distance depends entirely on pollination mechanism: wind and insect carriers need much larger distances than self-pollinators. Communities without large isolation distances can use time isolation (staggering planting dates) for wind-pollinated crops like maize.

right.text: 200-500 m from other maize varieties
5-10 m — almost no cross-pollination risk
500-1,000 m from other Brassica species
5-10 m adequate for most smallholder saving

exercises.prompt: Match each crop to its minimum seed-saving isolation distance.

exercises.explanation:
Condensation forms when moisture evaporating from beans condenses on cooler jar walls — confirming moisture content is still above the safe threshold (< 8% for legumes). Storing at this moisture in hermetic bags would lead to mould growth and loss of germination viability within months.

Why the other options are wrong: Condensation is a moisture warning, not a normal sign. In hermetic storage, high-moisture seed would create an anaerobic, humid environment that promotes mould even without oxygen — leading to mycotoxin contamination and seed death. Wood ash is added before sealing as a preventive measure, not as a cure for already-wet seed. The correct action is to break the seal, continue drying, then re-test before closing for storage. Condensation is a moisture indicator, not a temperature indicator. Cool seed does not produce condensation on inner jar walls unless moisture is being actively released.

options.text: Condensation is normal in sealed jars — proceed with hermetic storage immediately
Add wood ash immediately — ash will absorb the moisture inside the sealed jar
The beans are still too moist — continue drying in the sun for another 1-2 days, then repeat the jar test before sealing for long-term storage
The condensation indicates seed is sufficiently cool for storage — proceed

exercises.prompt: After 24 hours, a jar of dried beans sealed hermetically shows condensation on the inner walls. What does this mean and what action should be taken?

exercises.explanation: Documenting local variety diversity is the first step in community seed banking. Farmers' knowledge of variety performance under local conditions is irreplaceable and often exceeds formal breeding station data for smallholder-relevant traits like drought escaping and taste.
exercises.prompt: Visit a farm or market and photograph at least two different locally named crop varieties of the same species (e.g. two types of bean, two varieties of sorghum, or two local maize varieties). For each, record: local name, perceived advantages according to the farmer or seller (taste, drought tolerance, maturity time, storability), and any visible seed morphology differences (colour, size, shape).

rubric.criterion: Two clearly different varieties of the same crop species are photographed side by side
Local name of each variety is recorded
At least two farmer-perceived advantages per variety are documented
At least one visible morphological difference between varieties is described

lessons.outline: Open-pollinated variety (OPV) vs F1 hybrid — genetics, reproduction, and seed saving rules; positive mass selection — selecting 10-15% of best plants; isolation distances for cross-pollinating crops (maize 200-500 m, brassicas 500 m); seed drying to safe moisture content (< 12% for cereals, < 8% for legumes); hermetic storage and moisture indicators; seed viability testing (germination rate test); community seed bank design; variety trial methodology (mother-baby trial); labelling and record-keeping.
